justice: The space functions as a shared access road with no clearly marked pedestrian sidewalk, which concentrates usable space in a single carriageway and can disadvantage slower users (children, people carrying goods, etc.).
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or other barrier-free cues are present at edges/entries; the pond-side edge has a low curb and railing but not an accessible, continuous pedestrian facility.

Wayfinding and rule communication are minimal (only scattered caution cones), so expectations for who has priority (pedestrians vs. vehicles vs. bikes) are unclear, reducing perceived fairness for all users.
safety: There is no physical separation between walking space and vehicle space; the narrow lane and absence of a sidewalk increases pedestrian–vehicle conflict risk, especially around the bend ahead.
The waterside edge has a low railing/kerb next to the canal/pond; a slip or misstep on the narrow grass strip could lead to a fall into the water, especially in wet conditions.
Sightlines are partially constrained by trees and building masses near the mid-ground, and the lane appears to curve, reducing reaction time for drivers meeting pedestrians or cyclists.
livability: Residential buildings and visible greenery create a neighborhood-setting that can support daily life, but the street itself lacks amenities (no benches, no active frontage) that invite staying.
The area appears quiet with limited traffic volume (few parked cars visible and no heavy traffic), which can support a calmer living environment for mixed road users.
The canal/pond and adjacent green strip add a recreational and visual resource, yet there is no continuous promenade path, limiting how comfortably people can use it for everyday walking.
sustainability: Substantial tree and shrub presence on the left and mid-ground provides ecosystem services (shade, air quality, habitat), supporting environmental sustainability.
The canal/pond and vegetated edge indicate blue-green infrastructure, which can contribute to cooling and stormwater management compared with fully paved streets.
However, the road surface is largely impervious concrete and there are no visible permeable paving, bioswales, or rain gardens along the lane to manage runoff more effectively.
aesthetics: The combination of mature trees and the waterside view provides a pleasant natural scene that improves overall visual quality.
Building facades are visually consistent in height and color, but the environment feels utilitarian due to exposed overhead cables and the plain, wide concrete roadway.
The worn wall surfaces and scattered cones reduce perceived tidiness and visual coherence along the corridor.
comfort: Thermal comfort is moderate: trees and shrubs provide some shade, but large parts of the lane are exposed to sun with limited overhead canopy coverage on the roadway itself.
Physical comfort is limited by the lack of dedicated pedestrian paving and resting infrastructure; there are no benches or widened shoulder areas for stopping without blocking movement.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the quiet setting and greenery feel calming, but the proximity to water with a low barrier and the need to share space with vehicles can create stress for many users.
walkability: Walking is possible on the wide concrete surface, but there is no marked or raised sidewalk, so pedestrians must mix with vehicles along the entire segment.

The route appears continuous and relatively flat, yet the waterside edge and curb transitions are not designed as a continuous pedestrian path (grass strip and railing/kerb interrupt comfortable walking lines).
Limited pedestrian-support features (no crosswalks, no pedestrian signage, no lighting visible) reduce walking attractiveness and perceived safety, especially at night.
bikeability: There are no bike lanes, sharrows, or signage indicating bicycle priority; cyclists would need to share the narrow lane directly with motor vehicles.
The corridor includes a curve and partial visual obstruction by vegetation/buildings, which increases passing/meeting risk for cyclists and drivers.
No bicycle parking or end-of-trip facilities are visible near the buildings or along the route, reducing cycling convenience for everyday access.
